examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061894/assets/ffaf242238a8d32ce0f134cff6e0cf4256b2888b0a71f65e3c5ec470cbce284a.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above and the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle 2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}, \: e^{y/3} + 3x \right\rangle.$ 
Find a repeated integral in plane polar coordinates that's equivalent to $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \, .$
examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left( e^{y/3} + 3x \right) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061894/assets/e4c7913793a4b08916a832e575c5b2c167d5dfeec244eea23857731df1e514e7.png)

Since $P(x,y)= 2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}$ and $Q(x,y)=e^{y/3} + 3x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2y+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x+5}))\,dx+({e}^{y/3}+3x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨{y}^{3}+{e}^{x},\,\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}+10}-{x}^{3}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({y}^{3}+{e}^{x})\,dx+(\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}+10}-{x}^{3})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061894/assets/3e378b8f7731dbdbc44c232e9b8703067f39a5b3f836934afcbacb57d47972b2.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{3}+{e}^{x}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}+10}-{x}^{3},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{3}+{e}^{x})\,dx+(\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}+10}-{x}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-3\cdot (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-3\cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(-3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}-3{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
